question: I want to study how the shift to remote work changed commuting patterns in mid-sized European cities between 2018 and 2023. What data can I actually get?

requirements.text: Origin–destination commuting flows at municipality level or finer
Records the transport mode (car, public transport, cycling, walking)
Licence allows work with a commercial partner

record.title: Quillhaven Mobile Network Commuting Matrices, 2018–2023
record.description: Monthly origin–destination matrices of home-to-work movements between 214 municipalities, derived from anonymised mobile network signalling data and scaled to census population. Flows below 15 commuters are suppressed. Released as one table per month with municipality codes, flow counts and a confidence band.

notes: licence filled from the registry record

datasets.why: Monthly flows between 214 municipalities for the whole period, counting every way of travelling, with 31 mid-sized cities among them. It does not say how people travelled.

R1.evidence: Data dictionary: "origin and destination municipality code"

R4.evidence: 31 of the 214 municipalities have 100,000 to 500,000 residents (municipality list, sheet 2)

R5.evidence: No mode field; signalling data cannot tell a car from a tram

access_steps: Create a free account on the Coppice repository
Accept the click-through terms of use on the dataset page
Wait for the account to be activated (one or two working days)
Download the monthly tables, or request the link to the full archive
caveats: Flows under 15 commuters are suppressed, which hides most links between small municipalities.
The operator's market share changed in 2021. The publisher rescaled the series, and the method note warns of a break of up to 4%.
Non-commercial and share-alike: tables you derive must carry the same licence.

papers.title: Fewer trips, longer trips: commuting after the remote-work shift in 214 municipalities
papers.note: Used the monthly matrices to estimate the change in commuting volume by city size.

papers.title: Validating mobile network commuting flows against census journey-to-work tables
papers.note: Validation study: agreement with census flows is high for links above 100 commuters and poor below 30.

record.title: Brackenmoor Open Transit Tap Aggregates
record.description: Daily counts of smart-card taps between pairs of stops and stations on bus, tram and suburban rail in the Brackenmoor region, published by the transport authority since 2017. Counts under 5 for a station pair are rounded up to 5.

notes: no registry record for this host; the landing page answered and lists the files

datasets.why: Free to download today and daily, so you can start at once. It covers public transport in one region only, which is one slice of commuting in three mid-sized cities.

R1.evidence: Stop-to-stop counts; the stop table gives the municipality of each stop

R4.evidence: Three cities in the size band, all in one region

R5.evidence: Bus, tram and rail are separated; car, cycling and walking are absent

R6.evidence: Counts per station pair and day

access_steps: Download the yearly CSV files; no account is needed
caveats: Taps are not commuters: one person tapping in twice counts twice, and paper tickets are not counted.
The fare system changed in March 2022, when tapping out became compulsory on trams.

papers.title: Station-level recovery of public transport demand after 2020
papers.note: Used the daily counts to date the return of peak-hour travel.

record.title: Vantry Metropolitan Smart-Card Journey Records: Trip-Level Extract with Pseudonymised Card Identifiers, Boarding and Alighting Stops, Fare Products and Transfer Chains, 2016–2024
record.description: Every smart-card journey on the Vantry network since 2016: boarding and alighting stop, time to the second, fare product and a pseudonymised card identifier that stays the same for the life of the card. Analysis is allowed only inside the transit office's secure environment; results are checked before they leave it.

notes: the landing page mentions "data sharing agreement"; confirm the access route on that page before applying

datasets.why: The richest source found: it follows the same card across years, so you can see individual commuters cut back. It is also the slowest to obtain, and it covers public transport in one metropolitan area.

R1.evidence: Boarding and alighting stop for every journey

R4.evidence: One metropolitan area; four of its municipalities are in the size band

access_steps: Ask your institution's research office whether it already has a framework agreement with the transit office
Obtain ethics approval for the project from your own institution
Have an authorised signatory sign the data sharing agreement
Complete the transit office's half-day training on working in the secure environment
Receive a login for the secure environment; data cannot be downloaded
caveats: No licence is stated: the data sharing agreement sets the terms, and it is negotiated with each institution.
Outputs are checked before release, which adds about a week to every export.
A new card gets a new identifier, so people who replaced a lost card look like new travellers.

papers.title: Who stopped commuting? Card-level evidence from a metropolitan transit network
papers.note: Followed 310,000 cards from 2019 to 2023 to separate people who travel less often from people who left the network.

record.title: Estermere Regional Travel Diary Microdata, 2017–2023
record.description: Person- and trip-level records from a continuous household travel survey. About 9,000 respondents a year report every trip made on one assigned day, with purpose, main mode, start and end municipality and departure time. From the 2020 wave on, respondents also report how many days a week they work from home.

datasets.why: Trip-level records with mode and purpose, and the only obtainable source that asks about working from home directly. The sample is small for a single city, so flows between pairs of municipalities are noisy.

R1.evidence: Start and end municipality are recorded, but with about 9,000 respondents a year most municipality pairs have fewer than 10 trips

R2.evidence: Waves 2017 to 2023; fieldwork paused from April to August 2020

R3.evidence: Interview month is recorded; a monthly sample is about 750 respondents

R4.evidence: The sample covers 12 cities in that size band (sampling report, table 3)

R7.evidence: The End User Licence does not mention commercial use; the archive decides such requests case by case

access_steps: Register with the Estermere Social Data Archive using an institutional e-mail address
Submit a project description of about 300 words and name everyone who will handle the data
Sign the End User Licence online
Wait for archive staff to approve the application
Download the files from your archive account
caveats: Each respondent reports one day only, so the data cannot follow one person's commute over time.
No fieldwork from April to August 2020: the first months of the shift are missing.
Students need a supervisor to co-sign the application.

papers.title: Working from home and the weekly rhythm of travel: evidence from seven survey waves
papers.note: Compared commuting days per week before and after 2020 using the trip records and the working-from-home question.

papers.title: Télétravail et mobilité quotidienne dans les villes moyennes
Sample design and weighting of the Estermere travel diary
papers.note: Method report. Explains why monthly estimates for single cities are unreliable.

record.title: Pellwater Employer Commute Survey, 2019–2022
record.description: Yearly survey of 1,400 employers on where their staff live, how they travel to work and how many days they work remotely. The registry record describes the survey, but the files are under embargo and no release date is given.

datasets.why: It asks employers how many days their staff work remotely, which no flow dataset can tell you. Listed so that you know it exists: the record is real, but the files cannot be obtained today.

R1.evidence: Home and workplace are recorded by postal district, not municipality

R2.evidence: 2019 to 2022: one year before 2020, and the last wave is 2022

R4.evidence: The record does not list the places covered

R5.evidence: Abstract: "usual mode of travel to work"

access_steps: Nothing can be requested yet: the files are under embargo
Write to the data steward named on the record and ask to be told when the embargo ends
caveats: An open licence does not make the data available: the licence applies once the files are released.
No release date is given anywhere on the record.

problems: no registry searched lists a dataset with this title

datasets.why: Hourly counts of cyclists at 38 fixed counters could show whether cycling to work grew. It has no origins or destinations, and the page could not be reached.

R1.evidence: Counts at fixed points; no origin or destination

R3.evidence: Hourly counts, according to the paper that cites it

caveats: Known only from a citation in a 2022 paper; the address given there no longer answers.

papers.title: Counting commuters on two wheels: a bias check for automated cycle counters
papers.note: Names the feed as its data source. This is where the address came from.

not_recommended.name: Hollowbrook Freight Corridor Counts
not_recommended.reason: Counts goods vehicles on motorways only. It has no commuting trips and no origin–destination pairs, so it fails R1.

not_recommended.name: Marrowick Household Travel Snapshot 2016
not_recommended.reason: A single survey wave from 2016, so it cannot show change across 2020 and fails R2.

not_recommended.name: Tidewell Ride-Hailing Sample
not_recommended.reason: Mentioned in two papers, but no landing page or registry record could be found, so nothing about it can be checked.

gaps: No open, trip-level dataset covers both periods: every trip-level source needs an application or an institutional agreement.
Only one obtainable source records working from home directly. In the others, remote work has to be inferred from the fall in commuting trips.
Cities under 100,000 residents are missing from every dataset on this page.
notes: Sample report. Every dataset, publisher, registry, paper and link on this page is invented to show what a dataset-scout report looks like.
